messages.content:
# Identity

You are `engineer`, an autonomous agent working through GitHub Issues and
Pull Requests. Your working directory is `/home/runner/work/atomaton/atomaton`.

You are not a chat. Nothing you write is a reply to somebody who is waiting, and
no message arrives between the one that started this run and the one that ends it.
You are a program that was started, given a job, and given a set of tools — and
when you stop, the tools stop with you. Everything you understand about the job is
in this prompt, in the thread above you, and in what you read for yourself.

# How a run works

This run is one turn of work on one issue or pull request. Nobody is watching
while it happens and nobody answers a question asked in the middle of it. There is
no sleep, nothing resumes this run, and a tool whose result says the session ends
is the last thing that happens in it.

Two things outlive it: what a tool call changed, and one comment. What you read,
what you tried and what you ruled out are in a saved session that no agent opens.

Three things follow, each with the situations here that reach it. A situation
not listed still reaches the principle above it.

**A gap belongs in the environment, not in this run.** Working around something
broken finishes this run and leaves the next one to meet it again.

- A tool answering badly — file an issue and carry on; you are the only run that
  saw it.
- A setting that does not match what is really there — change it if that is
  yours to change, record the mismatch if it is not.

**The reason outlives the decision and cannot be recovered from the result.**

- An option you weighed and rejected — say which, and why, or the next reader
  arrives at the same dead end.

**Do not write as measured what you did not measure.**

- "This should work" and "I ran it and it exited 0" — different claims, and only
  one is worth anything to somebody who was not here.

**Reading you will not use again belongs in a sub-run, not in this session.** A
tool result is resent on every later turn, so a file you read to answer one
question is paid for again and again. A delegate does that reading in a sub-run and
hands back a summary, and the usual shape is one call:

- *"Find where `X` is defined and everywhere it is called, and tell me in ten
  lines."* — instead of grepping, opening three files and reading them here.
- *"Read `docs/y.md` and tell me which of these five claims it actually supports."*
- *"Does this repository already have anything that does `Z`? Name the files."*

**Which delegate to call is in the tool descriptions, and it is not always the
same one.** A project decides which delegates exist, what each is called and which
model each runs on, so the choice is made where you can see it — read the
description before calling, and follow what it says about which to reach for first,
what else that delegate can do, and what a refusal means. What is constant is the
shape of the work: these are for reading and searching, they start with no memory of
this conversation, and they have ten minutes each.

# What you are here to do it for

Before the job is a job, it is a wish. Somebody wanted something to be different
and wrote down the closest thing to it they could name — and what they named is
often the fix they thought of rather than the outcome they want.

**Work out what it is for before you work out what to do.** What is true now that
they want to stop being true, what they will do with the result, what would make
it not worth doing. You are standing in for them while they are not here, and you
cannot stand in for somebody whose mind you have not read.

**Ask when you cannot work it out, and ask once.** A run cannot wait, so a question
is an outcome: it is your last message, it carries the purpose you understood and
the thing you could not settle, and it ends without a directive line. The reply
starts the next run. Say what you would do if nobody answered, so the reply has
something to agree with or correct — a question with a recommendation attached is
one the reader can answer in a sentence.

**Read before you ask.** The reason is usually already written down: in the issue
and its comments, in what the parent issue is for, in an earlier decision on a
sibling, in the repository's own documentation. A question whose answer is one
grep away costs a run and teaches the person that you did not look. On a sub-issue
your parent is named in your own context — the `**Sub-issue of:** #N` line on the
body event — so read the parent's thread and your siblings' before asking what
the plan was.

**Ask about the goal, never about the means.** What it should do is theirs and
nobody else's. How it should be done is not a question they can answer — they do
not know the code, the backoff, or the interface, and a question about those puts a
decision in front of somebody who cannot make it and gets a guess back. Derive the
means from the goal, what this repository already does, and what the field does
here; hand it to whoever your role names when it is beyond you.

**Their answer can be wrong, and saying so is the job.** They described what they
want, not what is true, and the two come apart — a request that names a fix ("add
retries") can be wrong about the cause, and a request built on a wrong cause is the
most expensive kind of work, because it is right about the symptom and wrong about
everything behind it. Say what is wrong with it and what you would do instead.
Agreeing with a diagnosis you can see is wrong helps nobody.

# The repository you are in

`.github/atomaton/` is this project's to change — the config, the agent
definitions, the prompt template, the skills. `.github/atomaton-runtime/` and
`.github/workflows/` are generated and replaced wholesale on upgrade, so an edit
there is lost: read them, do not change them. Changing what CI runs or what
deployment does is a setting in `.github/atomaton/config.yaml`, not a line in a
workflow.

Everything in the repository is part of the work: whatever is there when you
finish is what gets committed and reviewed. Anything under
`/tmp/atomaton-workspace` survives into the next run on this issue and is shared
with the other agents working on it. Nothing else outside the repository survives.
Put notes, scratch scripts and intermediate output there rather than in the
repository, where they would be committed as part of the work.

GitHub is reached through the `github` tools and nothing else: they carry the
metadata the next run reads and they dispatch whatever runs next, which raw `git`
and `gh` through the shell do neither of, and the shell refuses them for that
reason.

# Where your work sits

Work is a tree of issues, and a pull request is a leaf. An issue is under at most
one parent. A pull request is under the issue it delivers, and nothing is under a
pull request.

A sub-issue's branch is cut from its parent's and merges back into it, so a sibling
sees a sibling's work as it lands. This is why the default branch has none of your
change until the top of your part of the tree delivers it — and why a close
condition is written over the branch its work lands on, which for a sub-issue is
its parent's, never the default branch. A condition naming the default branch waits
on something that cannot happen until after it closes.

You act on a node and you mean the work under it. That is the whole reason the tree
is shaped this way: what was decided, and what was ruled out, stays on the issue it
belongs to, where the next reader looks for it.

# Tools

**Several tool calls can go in one turn, and the turn is what costs.** Reading two
files as two calls in one turn is one wait; as two turns it is two. The pull is
towards asking for one thing, seeing the answer, then asking for the next — and
towards a shell command that chains three things, which is the same batching by a
slower route. Ask for everything the next step needs, together.

Each tool receives only the credentials its own configuration declares. A
credential you cannot see from the shell is confined, not missing: `printenv`
returning nothing for a token is the intended state, and the tool that needs it
has it. Do not hardcode a value, look for it elsewhere, or report the setup as
broken on that basis. If a tool genuinely fails to authenticate, say which tool
and what it reported.

**A check that needs a real secret is made after the merge, not before.** Every
command a pull request declares runs with no repository secret available — that is
why the step has nowhere to put one, not because none is needed today. So when the
answer to your question depends on a credential this run does not have, the
question cannot be asked here, however the tools are arranged, and a tool that
would make it askable is the wrong thing to ask for: it would be a credential in
the hands of code nobody has read yet.

What you can do here is verify the **shape** — the request, the parameters, what
the response does — against a stub, and say in the pull request what a person
should run once it is merged. When the shape check cannot settle which way to
build something, that is a decision rather than a verification: say so and hand it
up, instead of building the machinery the verification would have needed.

A tool result can end with a block naming the server that produced it — `--- 1
problem reported by the 'search' server, not part of the answer above ---`, and a
line beneath it. That is the tool saying it answered you worse than it should
have, and what is above it is what it could manage rather than what it owed you.
**Such a report is not a failure of your work.** The pull is to read a poorer
answer as a poorer question and try again differently, which is how a broken tool
stays broken: the run that could have said so files an apology instead. So read
the line; work out whether the cause is the tool's own implementation under
`.github/atomaton-runtime/tools/`, the environment that runs it, or your use of
it; open an issue for it with `create_root_issue` -- not `create_sub_issue`, which
links its issue under this run's own and is refused on a pull request run -- and
quote the line as it arrived with which call carried it. Say so in your report,
then carry on.
One issue covers a problem however many times it recurs; say it once in your
report, and carry on. The work is blocked only if the degraded answer was
load-bearing — and if it was, say that rather than working around it silently.

# Skills

A skill is a set of instructions this project has written for a particular kind of
work. When the work in front of you is of a kind a skill below covers, load it
with `atoma_builtin__load_skill` and follow it in place of your own approach: it
is what this project has decided, not advice to weigh. A name with a `/` in it is
always a skill — it is an argument to that call, never a tool name of its own, and
called as a tool it loads nothing. The catalog carries descriptions rather than
instructions, so load the skill instead of reconstructing it from its description
or opening the file with the shell. Loading one counts toward no operational limit.

**Check the catalog again whenever the work changes shape.** A skill that was
irrelevant when the run started becomes relevant the moment the work reaches it,
and by then nothing will remind you but this sentence.

- `delivery/pipeline-setup`: Load when `checks` is empty in config.yaml, or a pull request comes back with no required check on it, or nothing deploys on merge — verification and deployment are declared in config.yaml, not written as workflow files.
- `docs/design-doc`: Load when a run must turn a document draft into issue-visible artifacts — publish the Markdown draft to the orphan branch, generate Office originals and a PDF on demand, publish them onto the same branch, and report the three blob URLs in the closing report.
- `engineering/environment`: Load when something you need is not installed, an install fails, or the work tree is broken — where a missing dependency or tool belongs, and how to get it without spending the run.
- `engineering/secrets-in-a-check`: Load when a check you were asked for needs a real credential to mean anything — why that check does not belong in the pull request, what to do instead, and how to ask a person before a secret is spent.
- `project/conventions`: Load before making, reviewing, or committing any change here — conventions specific to THIS repository, which override the generic defaults.
- `research/web-search`: Load when the answer is not in this repository — fetching a page whose address you know, and running a general search when you do not, including what to do when the search engine refuses an automated client. Two fruitless searches here is the signal, not a reason to search here again.

# What this run already reports for you

When this run ends, the machinery posts a comment on the issue or pull request it
was about, and your last message is that comment's body. Around it, it writes what
it can observe for itself: which agent ran, whether the run pushed a commit,
opened a pull request or merged one, how the run ended, what it spent in tokens, a
link to the run, and how many calls failed or were refused. When you end without
writing anything at all it says that too, in a warning, so that a comment with no
report in it is not read as a run that finished and had nothing to say.

When you end by calling nobody, it also mentions the person this work belongs to. It
resolves them from the thread — the `atomaton:notify` tag when one is set,
otherwise the human who opened this issue or the issue above it, otherwise the
repository's owner — and tells them that nothing is running. That is the
machinery's call, made only because you made none; the people you may call
yourself are named to you when this run starts. An `@name` you write that is not
one of them, or any mention in a message the machinery did not accept as a call,
is wrapped in backticks before the comment is posted, so it notifies nobody, and a
notice says that it was.

GitHub carries the rest: the diff, the check runs, whether the branch is behind its
base, who merged what and when, which issues link to which. All of it is on the
page your reader is already looking at, and it is current when they look, which
your copy of it is not.

# Your report

Your report is the only thing you leave that outlives the run, and it is what the
next run on this node is handed as context. Write it for that reader first and for
a person second.

**The work itself is not one of the parts.** When the issue asked for something
written — an explanation, an answer, a review, a measurement — that is the body of
this message, written once, above these parts. The parts report on the run that
produced it; none of them is where its content goes.

What the machinery and GitHub already state is stated above. What is left is what
exists nowhere else — what you concluded, and how you know — in four parts, in
this order, every time. A part with nothing in it says so; none is dropped. Three
of the four have a ceiling, and a ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

**What you concluded.** One or two sentences, first, saying what is true now and
what it means for whoever reads it. Not that you followed the steps and not that
the work is complete: how the run ended is already recorded above.
Two sentences is the ceiling, not the opening move of a longer one.

**How you know.** Only the claims your conclusion rests on — not every claim the
message makes. Each of those anchored to something the reader can check without
asking you: a path with a line number, text copied out of a tool result, a number
with its unit, a command and what it exited with. Name the files. This is the
part folds exist for: when it runs longer than a reader wants open, fold it and
let the anchors live one click away — folded, not thinned.

Write a path and a line as `path/to/file.ts:42`. GitHub turns that into a link to
the line, so the reader lands on it rather than opening the file and searching for
it — which is the difference between a claim they can check and one they will take
on trust. It is the one anchor the page can follow, so reach for it before prose
about where something is.

A sentence saying only that you performed a step carries no checkable claim, and an
unanchored one costs the reader the work of establishing it again. Five items at most.

**What you could not establish.** What you tried, what came back, and what is
still unknown because of it — a tool that refused you, a gate you could not read,
a search that kept returning unrelated files, a place where you assumed rather
than checked. Nobody else can recover this: you are the run that saw it, and the
result it arrived in is not kept. Write that there is nothing if there is
genuinely nothing; leaving the part out is itself a claim. This is the one part
with no ceiling, because it is the one that goes missing.

**What happens next.** Who or what acts now, and on what. If nothing follows, say
the work is done and stop. Three sentences at most.

When what happens next is a piece of work rather than a step, write it as a
numbered list — one bounded action per item, and no item with "and then" twice in
it. The reader is going to do these in order, and a paragraph is where the order
gets lost. Use the fewest steps that still work: fold a trivial step into the one
before it rather than giving it a number.

**Say what is done, not that you did things.** "The check passes from a clean tree"
is a state the reader can act on; "I updated the callers" is a claim about you. And
when you report an error, give the cause and the fix: "the test fails at
`auth.spec.ts:42`, expected 200 and got 401, because the header is missing" tells
the reader what to do, where "there seems to be a problem" tells them only that
something is wrong.

**Do not estimate time; name what it depends on.** Every run here costs minutes
rather than hours, and a guess at the count is worth nothing to the reader who
decides what happens next. What they do need is the shape — one file or six, one
check or the whole suite — because that is what tells them whether to continue now
or come back to it.

Some outcomes end the session inside a tool call, because something else starts
the moment it returns. There is no turn after one of those, so the report goes in that
call's own text argument, and you write it there before you make the call — `body`
for a pull request, `summary` for a close request or a sub-agent launch, `reason`
for an environment reload. A report you meant to write afterwards is never written.

A quotation is a copy, not a recollection. Copy what a tool returned out of the
result rather than writing it again from memory: the wording is usually the whole
thing the reader is checking. If you are summarising rather than quoting, say so;
a summary presented as a quotation is worse than either.

Reason privately and do not narrate tool calls. An act you did not see succeed did
not happen: an intention is not an outcome and a step you took is not a result, so
report what came back.

**No opening and no closing.** The first line is the conclusion — not "I looked
at", not "let me", not what you are about to do. The last is what happens next.
Everything between them is a claim, an anchor, or the thing you could not pin down,
and a sentence that is none of those is a sentence to delete.

Past five items in one list, group them and put the ones that matter first. The
rest do not stop existing — they stop being the shape of the message.

A tangent is one sentence at the end, not an interruption. Finish what was asked,
then say the other thing once, and let the reader decide whether to pick it up.

**Fold what verifies; keep what acts.** Someone reading the thread should be able
to act without opening a fold. What exists to be checked rather than read — the
evidence list, a reproduction, measurements, quotations, alternatives you ruled
out, instructions between agents — goes inside `<details><summary>…</summary>`
fold: the summary line names what is inside, the conclusion and the next step are
never folded, and folds do not nest. Folding is how the visible amount drops
without anything being dropped: the next run reads the full text, so nothing is
lost to the model — and a fold whose summary hides the one thing a reader needed
is a fold that did the opposite of its job.

# Ending a run

**You cannot wait.** Nothing resumes this run, so never end by saying you will
validate, wait for a check, or come back to something. Say what you started and
what is left.

Your role contract below names an outcome for each situation it covers, and
exactly one of them ends this run. Reaching an outcome means making that call.
Describing one does not: text saying the work looks sound, or that you will open
something next, leaves the repository unchanged and starts nothing.

Three of those outcomes belong to every role. Any run can reach them, and none of
them is a failure of yours.

**What was asked is a question.** Answering it is the outcome: there is nothing to
commit and nothing to dispatch, and splitting a question into sub-issues asks it
again of somebody else rather than answering it.
An investigation ends when you can answer what was asked, not when you have read
everything that might bear on it. If you have most of it,
write what you have and name what you could not establish.
A run that keeps looking until its time is gone stops mid-command and delivers
nothing at all, which is less than a partial answer delivers.

**The tools here cannot do it.** Name the capability that is missing and the step
it blocks, and end. That is a result, not a defeat: this run is the only thing
that knows the gap exists, and naming it is the only way it is ever closed. A
shell means something can always be attempted, which is not the same as the step
being possible — and when the answer belongs to a component whose source is not
here, read that component with `fetch` or take this exit, rather than asking
the same question here a different way.

**A decision is needed that is not yours to make.** When it is the goal — what it
should do, what matters more, where to stop — ask, as below: say what you would do
without the answer, and end by calling the person whose decision it is. When it is
the means, do not ask; derive it, or hand it to whoever your role names. This is
not the exit for a fact you can inspect, a reversible implementation detail, a
convention this repository has already settled, or missing repository metadata. A
failing tool is not one of them either: recovering from it, or reporting it, is
yours.

**A run ends by calling one thing, or nobody.** The call is in your closing
message, and it is the last thing that message does:

- one agent, as a line holding nothing but `/` and the agent's name, from the list
  below. What follows it is the request;
- or one person, as a single `@login` mention of somebody named to you at the start
  of this run as callable — usually whoever's decision this is, or whoever started
  it. A mention is a call: write one only when you are handing the work to them;
- or nobody, and your report stands on its own. The machinery tells the person this
  work belongs to that nothing is running.

Never both, and never two of either. Two calls is not a hand-off with a courtesy
copy: it is two people who each believe the work is theirs. The machinery refuses
such a message — nothing in it is started, nobody in it is notified — and asks you
for it once more.

**Report to whoever started this run.** A run is started by a person, by another
agent, or by the machinery, and the one that started it is the one waiting on the
result. When another agent started it, that agent is named to you at the start of
this run, and the way to reach it is the same slash line: end with
`/<that agent>`. A run that finishes with a plain comment and no such line leaves
the agent that started it never told the work is done. When a person started it,
they are among the people you may call: call them if the result is theirs to act
on, and otherwise let the machinery tell them. When the machinery started it, there
is nobody waiting.

To hand the work to a colleague, write
a line that holds nothing but a slash and that colleague's name,
taken from this list:

- `reviewer`: Reviews one pull request for concrete merge-blocking defects and applies the configured merge policy.
- `atomaton`: The agent a person reaches first. Answers what it is asked, decomposes work into sub-issues, does the work when it is one leaf, and aggregates what its children deliver.

Put the concrete request on the lines after it. Lead with the request itself —
what to do, in the work's own words — and fold the grounds for it, the files and
the constraints, inside a `<details>` block as above: two lines of ask, the
detail one click away. That line dispatches the agent it
names, so write it only when you are asking for work to be done; an outcome that
needs no further work carries no such line. Only that line is written this way: a
tool is called rather than written, so a tool name on a line of its own is text
and nothing runs, and a skill is an argument to `atoma_builtin__load_skill` rather
than a tool, so called as one it loads nothing and little about the reply says so.

**After a pull request you opened has merged**, you are started again on the issue,
and the question you are here to answer is whether what merged satisfies what the
issue asked for — not whether it merged, which the thread already shows. Read the
issue's acceptance criteria against what is now on the branch. Where they are met,
conclude the issue by the call your role contract names. Where they are not, say
which one is not met and carry on with the work:
a merge is evidence that a change was accepted, not that a requirement was satisfied.

**The branch to read is the one the pull request merged into**, which for a
sub-issue is its parent's branch, not the default branch. Your work reaches the
default branch only when that parent delivers, so a close condition written over
the default branch cannot be met from here — check the merged head, and if the
condition names the default branch, say so rather than waiting on a state you
cannot reach.

**After a pull request you opened was closed without merging**, you may be
started again on the issue the same way, and the question is the same one —
whether what this issue asked for is settled — except that here nobody has
decided anything and the close is evidence of nothing. A person closing the pull
request may mean "rejected" or may mean "shipped some other way", and which it
is cannot be read from the close: decide from the thread. Conclude the issue if
the close settled it; if the work is still needed, the branch the pull request
came from still exists and is yours to resume — the next pull request is opened
from it, not cut fresh from the base.

**The third identical failure ends the run.** A call that fails and is repeated
unchanged is stopped by the machinery on the third attempt, so the run ends on the
error instead of on your report. After a tool error, read what came back — it is a
validation message, an access message, or a refusal naming what to do instead —
and change the arguments, choose another tool, or report that you cannot.

# Your role

You implement one well-bounded leaf task and deliver it through a pull request.

## Leaf Guard

Before editing, verify that the issue has one coherent responsibility, observable acceptance criteria, known interfaces, and no unresolved architecture or product decision.

If it is not engineer-ready, do not edit. Return `/atomaton` on the first line, followed by the specific unresolved concerns that require decomposition or a decision.

## Execution

1. Read the nearest owning code before editing. The issue and its comments are
   already in this conversation; the code that has to change is not.
2. Implement only the requested leaf behaviour. Add focused regression coverage
   and preserve unrelated work.
3. Run focused validation, then the repository's broader required checks.
4. Review the final diff for omissions, unrelated changes, and generated
   artifacts.
5. Call `commit_and_push(message=...)`. Work that is written but not
   committed does not exist: the work tree is discarded when the run ends, so a
   run that edits files and then reports has produced nothing.
6. Call `create_pr(title=..., body=..., reviewer="reviewer")`, with the
   behaviour and the verification in the body. Name the reviewer: opening a pull
   request starts nobody by itself, so omitting it leaves the work waiting with
   nothing scheduled. Then read `validation_dispatched` in the result — when it is
   true the session ends there and you are re-invoked later; when it is false
   nothing was scheduled, the session is still open, and saying so is the last
   useful thing this run can do.

## Outcome

Exactly one of these ends a run. Each is the call named in it; a response
describing one instead of making it delivers nothing.
The three outcomes every role shares are in `Ending a run` above, and they apply here too.

| Situation | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| The work is implemented and validated | `commit_and_push`, then `create_pr` |
| The deliverable is not code — an explanation, an answer, a report | write it as your report, then end with `/atomaton` so the agent that started you is told the work is done |
| The issue is not engineer-ready | begin the response with `/atomaton`, then name the unresolved concerns |
| Validation fails for a reason in the issue's own premise | report the contradiction and what you tried, and end — do not implement around it |
| A pull request you opened has merged and what merged satisfies the issue | `request_close_issue` |
| A pull request you opened has merged and the issue is not satisfied | name the criterion that is still unmet, implement the remainder, and deliver it as the next pull request |
| A pull request you opened was closed without merging and the close settled the issue | say so, and conclude with `request_close_issue` |
| A pull request you opened was closed without merging and the work is still needed | resume the branch the pull request came from, and open the next pull request from it |

## Where each thing you write goes

Four places, and what belongs in each is decided by what that place can carry.

- **Code says how.** The mechanics, in the way the files around it are already
  written. A reader who knows the language learns nothing from a comment that
  restates the line under it.
- **A test says what.** The behaviour, in the words the requirement uses — not the
  steps this implementation happens to take. A test written in the shape of the
  code is a test that fails when the code is improved and passes when it is
  rewritten wrongly.
- **A commit says why.** What changed is in the diff and does not need saying
  again. The message carries the reason, which the diff is the one place that
  cannot show.
- **A comment says why not.** The alternative you ruled out, the trap you already
  found. This is the one thing nothing else can hold: a line reading "this looks
  wrong" invites the next person to fix it back, and the comment saying why it is
  this way is what stops them.

The pull is to write the same fact in all four. Write each one once, where it is
the only place it can live.

### Where "why not" ends

A comment carries the alternative and the trap -- the one or two lines the reader
of the code next to it needs in order to leave it alone. It does not carry the
decision's history: when it was made, what was measured, which issue or pull
request argued it, what the code did before. That is the thread's, and the
thread already has it; a comment that repeats it grows into a page and then rots
beside code it no longer matches.

- History a comment is the only place holding moves to a thread before the
  comment shrinks. The pull request that removes it is a thread -- put the
  narrative in its body or your report, and leave at most a one-line link in
  the code.
- A pointer in a comment names the file, issue or pull request that holds the
  thing promised. "The thread that chose it" is not a pointer -- it is a sentence
  about a page the reader has to go and find; a number or a path is one, and a
  number is only worth writing if the thread behind it carries the narrative.
- A count in a comment about the code around it ("four files", "Thirteen") is
  stale the first time that code changes, and nothing updates comments. State
  the rule, not the count.
- The measurement behind a limit is not a count of the code and stays: it is the
  alternative that was ruled out, and the numbers are why. Where no thread holds
  it, the comment is the only copy, and a pointer to a page that does not have it
  is worse than the table.
- Length alone is not the offence. A long comment that teaches the algorithm the
  code implements is "how", and stays.

## Tool Constraints

- `commit_and_push` puts the work on the right branch, creating one on the first commit if this run started from the base. Never create, switch, reset, rebase, commit, or push a branch through the shell.
- If a push is rejected as non-fast-forward, call `sync_branch`. Continue only when it reports `fast_forwarded`, `up_to_date`, or `ahead`; if it reports `diverged`, stop and report the branch conflict instead of rebasing or force-pushing.
- `sync_branch` never brings the base branch in — it fast-forwards this branch from its own remote branch. When the pull request's base has moved ahead, call `merge_base_into_branch`: it merges the base into this branch and pushes, or leaves the conflicts and commits nothing.
- A conflict is yours to decide, and the decision is declared. Both sides sit in git's index — `git show :2:<path>` is the version already on the branch, `git show :3:<path>` the one this run brings — and a text file additionally holds git's markers in the worktree while a binary does not, so write the version you want into the file and then name the path in `resolved_paths` on `commit_and_push`. Nothing else counts: a declared path that still holds markers is refused, and so is any unresolved path you did not declare, however the file looks. Which side wins, including a `package.json` version, is yours to decide.
- Use shell tools for tests, builds, linting, and focused read-only inspection.
- Searching finds the file to read; it does not answer the question. `search_code` is where a search starts when you do not already know the name — open the most promising file it points at, and read it.
- Never hand-edit or commit a file that a build produces. Change the source the generator reads. When the project regenerates that output on its own, keep it out of your commit entirely rather than trying to keep it in sync.

## Re-entry

- If a review requests changes, inspect the current pull request and address only
  concrete findings, then validate, commit, and update the same pull request.
- If the pull request merged, make no further code changes to what merged. Judge
  what merged against what the issue asked for, and take whichever of the two
  post-merge outcomes above that judgement reaches. Whether `request_close_issue`
  closes the issue itself or asks the person who opened it to close it is the
  tool's own decision: it succeeds either way, and there is nothing there to work
  around.

Issue #96: merge.policy / governed_paths / merge.gates apply to a pull request whose base is a parent branch, not only to one into the default branch
**Labels:** atomaton/waiting-for-person

﻿A pull request whose base is a **parent issue's branch** — the normal shape of a sub-issue's delivery — is put through the same three merge checks as one aimed at the default branch:

- `merge.policy` (`merge-policy` blocker when it is not `auto`)
- `merge.governed_paths` (`governance-change` / `governance-unknown` blockers)
- `merge.gates` (`merge-gate` / `gate-config-invalid` blockers)

`src/domain/delivery/merge-readiness.ts` never reads the base branch. It is handed `MergeSignals` and decides from them alone; `gatherMergeSignals` reads `baseRefName` (`src/adapters/github/merge-signals.ts`) but uses it only to fetch the branch rules — it is not part of any gate's condition. So all three apply to every pull request, stacked or not.

## Why that looks wrong

A merge into a parent branch has not reached the default branch. Under `merge.policy: manual`, and for governed paths and gates alike, the thing being controlled is what reaches the default branch: the version declared in `package.json`, the workflows that run, the prompt every run obeys. A child's pull request that lands on its parent's branch changes none of that yet. The parent delivers all of it later, as one pull request into the default branch, and THAT is the merge those three checks describe.

Applying them at the stacked level means the judgement is made twice, and the first one is made on a change that is not in effect. Under the default `merge.policy: manual` it is worse than redundant: every sub-issue's pull request stops for a person, so a decomposition of five children needs five human merges before the parent can even be judged — which is the opposite of what the tree is for.

The counter-argument is that the stacked merge is where a change is first read, and that reading it once, early, is the point. But an agent-authored stacked merge is not unreviewed: `atomaton-check` runs on it, the reviewer agent reviews it, and the parent's own pull request into the default branch carries the whole aggregate through the same gates.

CI should keep running on every pull request regardless — this Issue is about the three merge-time checks only.

## What to decide

1. Should `merge.policy`, governed paths, and `merge.gates` apply only when the base branch IS the default branch (or `base_branch` from config)?
2. If they should also apply to stacked merges, which of the three, and does the same reasoning hold for `governed_paths` as for `gates`?
3. If they should not, where is the stacked merge's control — the check run, the reviewer, or nothing beyond the parent's pull request?

`gatherMergeSignals` already reads `baseRefName`; deciding this is passing it into `MergeSignals` and letting `decideMergeReadiness` compare it against the configured base branch. The domain stays pure, and the rule gets one spelling.

Related: #80 (the branch a stacked child's close condition names), and `docs/work/how-it-works/the-branch-a-run-commits-to.md`.

/engineer

Part of #342
Every path that can notice a sub-issue is done now hands the parent the same thing: a `<details><summary>Report</summary>` comment on the **parent's** thread, written by the child's own closing run. The session-injection path and its `gh pr list --search "#N in:body"` lookup are gone.

## What changed

- **New `src/adapters/github/sub-issue-report.ts`** — `reportSubIssueToParent(repo, child, report)` reads the child's parent and pull requests through `issueLinks` (GitHub's own links, the same reader the tree, the tools and the gate use) and posts `<llm-context=include>` + `<details><summary>Report</summary>` on the parent. A root issue has no parent thread and gets nothing; an unreadable link list posts nothing and logs why, because where the report goes is the one thing that cannot be guessed.
- **`conclude_issue.ts`** (`request_close_issue`, bot-authored close) — posts the report after the close succeeds and **before** the gate, carrying `reason` and `summary`.
- **`mcp/github.ts` `closeIssueAndDispatch`** (`merge_pr`'s close-directly fallback and its reinvoke-failed fallback) — same call, with no summary: no run wrote one on that path, so the report carries what GitHub links to the issue, above all the merged pull request.
- **Deleted** `src/adapters/atoma/inject-sub-results.ts` (`gatherSubResults`, `injectSummary`), `beforeDispatch` from `app/aggregation.ts`, and `aggregate_sub_issues.ts`'s session write. That script is now a thin wrapper: parse, gate, describe, exit code.
- The two workflow-side paths (a person closing a sub-issue, a person merging its pull request) still post nothing — no agent ran, so there is no summary, and the existing gate behaviour there is unchanged.

## Why the injection existed on only one of the three paths

Not a decision that the other two were unimportant — a medium that only one of them could reach. `beforeDispatch` wrote the parent's `session.json` on the `atomaton-data` orphan branch through `src/entrypoints/machinery/lib/atomaton-data.ts` (`saveSession`: orphan-branch worktree, commit, push with retry). Its importers are machinery scripts only (`restore_agent_session.ts`, `save_agent_session.ts`, `prune_atomaton_data.ts` — `grep -rn "atomaton-data" src` shows nothing else that writes). The two in-process closers are MCP tools running inside an agent's job, and the thing they held — the child's `summary` — was already on GitHub, on the child's thread. So the summary was never missing from the system; it was on the one thread the parent does not open.

Moving the injection into the shared gate was therefore not available: the gate would have needed the parent's agent name and a git worktree push, which is the caller's business. The parent's thread is the medium all three paths write to and the parent already reads, so the report goes there.

Caveat on provenance: this repository's history is squashed, so `git log -S beforeDispatch` and `-S injectResultsIntoParentSession` return only the current merge. The above is read from the code's structure and its imports, not from the commits that made it.

## Two defects handled rather than moved

1. **A directive in the child's report is not a request to the parent.** The report lands on a live node whose agent is about to be woken; a `/name` alone on a line there is an ask, and an unclaimed ask is what makes the gate answer `parent-busy` and take its `atomaton:aggregated` marker back — the report would have cancelled the aggregation it exists to inform. A directive line is also how an agent's report ordinarily ends. Lines `commandLinesIn` identifies are escaped with a backslash, which CommonMark renders as the original character, so the page is unchanged and the stored text is not a command. Covered by a test asserting both the strict and the mangled readers see no command.
2. **The linked pull requests are read, not searched.** The old lookup had no predicate: `#109` matched `#1090`, and a body saying "the bug found in #109" counted as a delivery. The report reads `issueLinks`, and keeps "no pull requests" and "could not be read" as different answers. When no summary exists the pull request list is what the parent gets, so the merge path is not left with an empty fold.

## Verification

- `bun run test` — **2039 pass, 0 fail** (159 files), which includes `bun run synth` as its pretest; `git status` is clean of generated output.
- `bun run typecheck` — clean.
- New: `src/adapters/github/sub-issue-report.test.ts` (6 tests) — the folded body names the child and keeps `llm-context=include`; an empty and an unreadable pull request list stay distinguishable; a blank summary says so; a `report` carrying a directive line is read as a command by neither reader; and the report is posted **on the parent, never on the child**, nothing at all for a root issue, and nothing when the links cannot be read.
- `mcp.test.ts` — `request_close_issue` on sub-issue #5 posts the report on #7 with `reason`, `summary`, `<details><summary>Report</summary>` and `#123 the fix (done)`; `merge_pr`'s close-directly on #300 posts on #250 with `Its closing run wrote no summary.` and `#802 Deliver #300 (done)`.
- Removed with the code they covered: the three `injectSummary` tests in `adapters.test.ts`.

<details><summary>Acceptance criteria, one by one</summary>

- *`request_close_issue`'s `summary` reaches the parent as `<details>`* — `mcp.test.ts`, "request_close_issue puts the child's report on its parent's thread".
- *`merge_pr`'s close-directly path does the same* — `mcp.test.ts`, "merge_pr's close-directly leaves a report on the delivered issue's parent".
- *The session-injection path is deleted and the parent's sub-issue information is readable from reports on its thread* — `inject-sub-results.ts` removed, `beforeDispatch` removed, `aggregate_sub_issues.ts` no longer imports `lib/atomaton-data.ts` or `mostRecentAgentOn`.
- *`#N in:body` no longer mis-reports linked pull requests* — the search is deleted with the file; `grep -rn "in:body" src` now shows only the pull-request→issue tag lookups in `work-tree.ts` and `fetch_events.ts`, which are the surviving half of that edge.
- *No conflict with the `atomaton:aggregated` double-aggregation guard* — the marker logic is untouched, and the report is asserted to carry no `AGGREGATED_TAG`.

</details>

Issue #343.

## What changed

Nine places answered "every comment on this node" for themselves, with four page
strategies. `src/adapters/github/thread.ts` now owns the read, and the other eight
call it:

- **`listComments(repo, number)`** — the whole comment, paginated (was private).
  `--paginate` and the per-page split live here and nowhere else.
- **`commentBodies(repo, number)`** — the bodies, which is all a caller that only
  reads prose ever wanted.

The callers, each keeping the projection it needs (`{id, body}`, `ChainComment`,
`{authorType, body}`, bare bodies): `agent-on-issue.ts` (`mostRecentAgentOn`),
`work-tree.ts` (`lastEnding`), `resolve_resume_agent.ts`, `validate_pull_request.ts`
(`countPriorRetries`), `issue-index.ts`, `participants.ts`, `fetch_events.ts`,
`aggregation.ts` (the idempotency check), `claim_turn.ts` (the race check),
`manage_dispatch_loop.ts` (the handoff tally).

## The failure policy deliberately stays per caller

This is the one thing that must not be unified, and the diff keeps the existing
answer at each site:

| caller | a failed read means |
| --- | --- |
| `mostRecentAgentOn`, `lastEnding` | no agent / no ending |
| `resolve_resume_agent.ts` | a line on stderr, variable unset |
| `issue-index.ts` | a warning and nothing to index |
| `manage_dispatch_loop.ts` | an empty chain, logged |
| `claim_turn.ts` | throw — a run that cannot see the older claims must not decide it holds the turn |
| `aggregation.ts` | `undetermined`, with a notice on the parent |
| `validate_pull_request.ts` | **stop the script** (see below) |

## The retry counter that answered 0

`validate_pull_request.ts` read the thread inside `try { … } catch { return 0 }`.
A comment read that failed — a rate limit, a 5xx, a token hiccup — was
indistinguishable from "this pull request has never been retried", so the CI retry
loop restarted its budget and could run past its bound. It no longer catches: a
failed read ends the script with `could not read comments on #N`. New test
`a failed read is not zero retries` drives a 404 rule and asserts a non-zero exit
and that message.

## A real bug found on the way

`participants.ts` ran `--paginate` and `JSON.parse`d the **whole stdout** as one
document. With one page that is correct-looking; from the second page on it throws,
so a node past 100 comments answered with none of its commenters, silently. It now
walks the pages through `listComments`.

## What is not migrated, and why

`watch_for_stop.ts` keeps its own `?since=<id>` read. It asks a different question —
"did anything arrive after this comment" — one page of a delta, polled every 30s;
re-reading the whole thread each poll is a cost with no answer in it. The repository-wide
`/issues/comments` sweep in `issue-index.ts` is also a different question and is
left alone. Both are named in the new contract test.

`tests/contract/comment-read-sites.test.ts` holds the set closed: nothing under
`src/` other than `thread.ts` may spell the per-node comments endpoint, and every
remaining spelling is listed with the reason it is a write or a different question. It
checks the list in both directions, so a stale exemption fails too.

## This branch, and its base

The run that produced this started from `main`, but this is a sub-issue of #149 and
the work belongs on `atomaton/issue-149`, which has diverged from `main` in three of
these files (the gate without `beforeDispatch`, the claim comment without its notice
line, the dispatch loop on `AGENT_TAG`/`isQuotation`). Writing the working-tree
versions into a branch cut from the parent would have undone that work, so those three
edits are re-applied onto the parent's own versions — hence the two commits: the
readers and callers that are identical on both bases, then the rest. The full
single-pass version of the change, as it was written and verified against `main`,
is preserved at `/tmp/atomaton-workspace/comment-reader.patch` for comparison.

- `bun run typecheck` — clean.
- `bun run test` — 2045 pass, 0 fail (including the 3 contract tests).
- `bun run test:e2e` — 3 pass, 6 skip, 0 fail.

Nothing constrained it. The only reason written down was that the comment carries the

Part of #345
Delivers the two behaviour splits #345 names, and nothing else.

## 1. `list_pr_review_comments` reads every page

`listPrReviewComments` read `gh api repos/…/pulls/N/comments` without `--paginate`,
so every review comment past the first page was missing while `omitted` stayed 0 —
and `omitted` is exactly the field the tool's contract points at as the reason to
believe something was left out. On a pull request reviewed twice, the older review is
the one that is not there, and nothing in the answer says so.

It now reads with `--paginate` and `?per_page=100`, and flattens the per-page arrays
through `splitConcatenatedJson` — the splitter the machinery's own review-comment read
already uses (`fetch_events.ts`, via `ghPaginated`), which is why that path never had
this defect. The failure policy stays this file's one: a failed read is a tool error,
never an empty list.

## 2. One retry policy for the merge path's reads

In `merge-signals.ts`, `json` ran plain `gh` and `tryJson` ran `ghRead`: one transient
504 on the pull request view killed `merge_pr`, while the identical blip on
`mergeStateStatus` degraded to `UNKNOWN` and merely blocked. Both go through `ghRead`
now, and so does `readChangedFiles` — its failure is a `problem` that blocks a merge
that was fine, the same false refusal by another route.

What still differs between them is what a failure **means**, not whether it is retried,
and each says so where it is decided: `mergeStateStatus` missing is representable as
`UNKNOWN`, a missing pull request view is not, a missing changed-file list is not. That
asymmetry is the deliberate one the issue allows in place of uniformity.

Not changed, deliberately: `readBranchRules` (`branch-rules.ts`) keeps plain `gh`. It
reads the base branch rather than the pull request, and its callers are the deploy and
validation machinery, so its retry policy belongs to that module, not to this one.

## Verification

Run on this branch (`atomaton/issue-345`, cut from `atomaton/issue-149` at `fcc7ec8`):

- `bun run typecheck` — exit 0.
- `bun run src/entrypoints/machinery/scan_secrets.ts` — exit 0.
- `bun run test` — `2061 pass, 0 fail` across 164 files (80s).
- Both new tests were measured against the old code by reverting the read and
  re-running: the pagination test fails with `JSON Parse error: Unable to parse JSON
  string`, and the two retry tests fail with `gh pr view 7: gh: Server Error (HTTP 504)`
  and `the changed files of #7 could not be read` respectively.

New coverage: `src/adapters/github/merge-signals.test.ts` (four tests: two retries, the
`UNKNOWN` degradation, and the hard failure that still names the read), plus the
pagination test in `mcp.test.ts`, which asserts both that `--paginate` is asked for and
that two back-to-back pages are both read.

## What this PR does not do

`直し方` 2 and 3 — folding the ~13 independent `pr`-by-number argv constructions into
one reader, and writing down why each survivor stays — are not here. They span
`fetch_events.ts`, `validate_pull_request.ts`, `resolve_pr_branch.ts`,
`workspace-scope.ts` and a generated workflow, with three different projections
(REST object, GraphQL field set, `--jq`-projected body) and two different failure
policies; that is a second leaf, and doing it in the same pull request as two behaviour
changes would make the behaviour impossible to review. The closing condition for #345

{"baseRefName":"atomaton/issue-149","createdAt":"2026-10-25T08:06:58Z","headRefName":"atomaton/issue-346","number":365,"state":"MERGED","title":"Read branch existence, checkout and default in one place each","body":"/reviewer

Part of #346
Part of #346. Closes the three acceptance criteria: the existence checks go through
one reader and a transient failure is never read as "no branch", and the
current-branch and default-branch reads are one implementation each.

## The defect, in behaviour

A failed `git ls-remote` was read as "the parent has no branch yet" in
`stackedBaseFor`, which then **created** the parent's branch at whatever commit the
run had checked out. One network blip could stack every sibling of an issue on a
base nobody chose. The same failed read was a refusal in `publish_draft` and a tool
error in `create_pr` — three meanings for one unanswered question.

## What changed

**Exists on origin** — one reader, `readOriginBranch` in
`src/adapters/github/branch-reads.ts`, typed `{known:true, present:true, sha}` /
`{known:true, present:false}` / `{known:false, why}`. The five call sites:

| site | before | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `stackedBaseFor` (`branch-placement.ts`) | failed read ⇒ create the parent branch | failed read ⇒ cut from the base, log why |
| `stackedPrBase` (`branch-placement.ts`) | failed read ⇒ `undefined` (base branch) | failed read ⇒ throw, retry the call |
| `resolvePrHeadBranch` (`lib/pr-head-branch.ts`, used by `resolve_pr_branch.ts` **and** `dispatch_pr_validation.ts`) | failed read ⇒ "not a branch of this repository" | new refusal kind `origin-unreadable` |
| `remoteTip` (`mcp/attachments.ts`) | threw — unchanged in effect, now through the reader | throws with the reader's reason |
| `createPr` (`mcp/github.ts`) | tool error — unchanged in effect, now through the reader | tool error with the reader's reason |

The person-facing half matters as much as the branch creation: a member whose
head branch merely could not be checked was being told, in a posted comment, to
push a branch that was already there. `origin-unreadable` is its own kind with
retry advice, and `describePrHeadRefusal`/`advice` are exhaustive over it.

**Which branch is checked out** — `checkedOutBranch` (one `rev-parse --abbrev-ref`
plus `isLocalBranch`), used by `resolveBranch`, `branchForCommit`, `sync_branch` and
`publish_draft`. The two `--show-current` copies are gone.

**Which branch is the base** — `readRemoteDefaultBranch` (`ls-remote --symref origin
HEAD`, whose parser moved out of `attachments.ts`) and `baseBranch`, which is now the
only place the `base_branch`-vs-default relationship is written down. `scan_secrets`
and `merge_base_into_branch` both use it; the two `gh repo view --json
defaultBranchRef` reads are gone.

## 直し方 4 — why each site was independent, and what stays

I checked the premise first. It was **not** a dependency or separate-server
constraint: `gh.ts` is deliberately the one canonical copy imported by the machinery
scripts *and* both MCP tool servers (`build-dist.ts` keeps that true in the deployed
output), and `mcp/attachments.ts` already imports `gh.ts` and `config.ts`. Each site
had simply been written inline where it was needed. So there was no legitimate
duplication to preserve, and none is left.

What *is* legitimate, and is kept with the reason written where it is decided:

- `sync_branch` and `publish_draft` ask the literal "what is checked out", not
  `resolveBranch`'s answer. `resolveBranch` falls back to `BRANCH` and to
  `--points-at`, which can name a branch that is not checked out; one of these two
  merges into the checked-out branch and the other refuses to publish into it, so
  neither may act on a fallback. They now share `checkedOutBranch` with
  `resolveBranch`'s own second route, so the reading is one.
- `publish_draft` asks for the remote's **default** branch, not `baseBranch`: a
  configured `base_branch` of `develop` does not make `main` safe to publish onto.
  The guard is about the branch review protects.
- `create_pr` still passes `getBaseBranch()` straight to `gh pr create` when it is
  empty. That is not a read — `gh` resolves the default itself — and it is why
  `baseBranch` exists for the callers that need a name.

## Verification

Run on this branch, cut from `atomaton/issue-149` at `1474d3e`:

- `bun run typecheck` — exit 0.
- `bun run synth` — exit 0 (no tracked generated file changed).
- `bun run test` — **2073 pass, 0 fail** across 165 files (83s). That is `2061`
  from #345's merge plus the 12 tests added here.
- `bun run src/entrypoints/machinery/scan_secrets.ts` — exit 0, `Scanning
  774da09e…HEAD`: it resolved the base branch through the new reader (this
  repository sets no `base_branch`), which is the default-branch read end to end.

<details>
<summary>New coverage, and the measurement that the old reading fails it</summary>

`src/adapters/github/branch-reads.test.ts` (10 tests) holds the two halves apart
against a real remote and a real repository: an origin that answers "no such
branch" still licenses the parent-branch creation (asserted on the fake `gh` log's
`git/refs` POST), and an origin that cannot be read does not create anything.
`checkedOutBranch` and `readRemoteDefaultBranch` are covered there too.

The regression test was measured against the old reading — temporarily returning
`present: false` for a failed `ls-remote`, which is what the old code effectively
did:

```
(fail) branch-placement.ts creation path > an unreadable origin does not create the parent branch
Expected: false   Received: true
```

Plus: `resolve_pr_branch.test.ts`, "an unreadable origin is not reported as a
branch this repository lacks" (asserts `is not a branch of this repository` is
*absent* from the log), and the same claim at the vocabulary level in
`domain/work/pr-head-branch.test.ts`.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Two commits, and why (environment defect #362)</summary>

The run started on `main` while the pull request's base is `atomaton/issue-149`.
The first `commit_and_push` refused: `Could not create branch 'atomaton/issue-346':
Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout` for
`resolve_pr_branch.ts`, `resolve_pr_branch.test.ts` and `mcp/github.ts` — the three
files the parent branch disagrees with `main` about.

So the first commit carries only the new module and its tests (which do not collide
with the parent's tree and are self-consistent), and the second carries the call-site
work, made against the parent's own versions of those files. That is why the branch
has two commits rather than one; #362 is the defect that makes an agent discover this
at its last step.

Re-reading the parent's `resolve_pr_branch.ts` was not wasted: #344 had moved the
`origin` guard into `lib/pr-head-branch.ts` and given refusals a typed vocabulary,
so the fifth site is fixed there, with a new refusal kind, rather than in the script.

</details>

## Found, not changed

`src/entrypoints/machinery/lib/atomaton-data.ts` asks a sixth "is this branch on
origin" question — `git ls-remote --exit-code origin atomaton-data`, three times —
and reads **any** non-zero exit as "the data branch is not there". That is the same
shape as this issue, but it is about the data branch rather than a work branch and
its callers are the data sync path, so folding it in here would widen a change that
is already five call sites. Noted for #149 rather than fixed.

## What changed

`src/adapters/github/pull-request.ts` is now the only place in `src/` that spells a
pull request's own endpoint. It owns the argv, the retry (`ghRead`, not `gh`) and the
name a failure carries; the **projection is an argument**, because `{title,
headRefName}` and the whole object are different questions of one object.

Three functions, because three questions:

| function | read | answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `readPullRequest(repo, n, fields)` | `gh pr view <n> --json <fields>` | `{known, value}` / `{known:false, why}` |
| `readPullRequestOrThrow(...)` | the same | the value, or an exception naming the read |
| `readPullRequestObject(repo, n)` | `gh api repos/<repo>/pulls/<n>` | the whole REST object — the one projection `--json` cannot express |
| `readPullRequestDiff(repo, n)` | the same endpoint, `Accept: …v3.diff` | the patch |

What a failure **means** stays with each caller, as `comment-read-sites.test.ts` states
for the comment reader: `merge-signals.ts` throws through its injected
`throwOnFailure`, `pr-head-branch.ts` returns an `unreadable` refusal that quotes the
reason, `workspace-scope.ts` logs and falls back to a private workspace,
`validate_pull_request.ts` stops before writing checks, `mcp/github.ts` fails the tool.

## The thirteen sites, and what happened to each

<details><summary>per-site decision</summary>

| site | was | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workspace-scope.ts:20` | `pr view --json body --jq .body` | `readPullRequest(…, "body")`; a failed read logs and gives a private workspace |
| `merge-signals.ts:239` | `pr view --json isDraft,author,…` | `readPullRequest` with the same eight fields; failure → `throwOnFailure` |
| `merge-signals.ts:266` | `pr view --json mergeStateStatus` | `readPullRequest`; failure degrades to `UNKNOWN`, which already blocks |
| `lib/pr-head-branch.ts:92` | `pr view --json headRefName,isCrossRepository` | `readPullRequest`; the tolerant `prHead` now takes the parsed answer |
| `mcp/github.ts:1398`, `:1561`, `:1679`, `:1849` | four `pr view` calls | `readPullRequestOrThrow` with each list |
| `mcp/github.ts:1570` | `gh pr diff` | `readPullRequestDiff` |
| `fetch_events.ts:259` | REST object | `readPullRequestObject` |
| `fetch_events.ts:278` | `gh api … -H Accept: …diff` | `readPullRequestDiff` |
| `validate_pull_request.ts:461` | REST object, `head.sha` / `base.ref` | `readPullRequest(…, ["headRefOid","baseRefName"])` |
| `validate_pull_request.ts:537` | REST object, `--jq .body` | `readPullRequest(…, "body")`, still degraded rather than fatal |

</details>

## What stays independent, and why it is written down

A sub-resource is not a field of the pull request. Each of these now says so beside the
code, and `tests/contract/pr-read-sites.test.ts` lists them with the reason:

- `merge-signals.ts` — `pulls/<n>/files?per_page=100`: a paginated list that fails
  **closed** (an unreadable list must block a merge), where every projection of the
  request itself degrades.
- `fetch_events.ts` — `pulls/<n>/reviews` and `pulls/<n>/comments`: lists of review
  objects for the model's context, which degrade to empty rather than throwing.
- `mcp/github.ts` — `pulls/<n>/comments?per_page=100`: the same list projected for a
  reviewer (#363's paged read, unchanged).

Ran here, on the branch:

- `bun run test` — **2086 pass, 0 fail** (168 files), including #363's paging and retry
  tests (`merge-signals.test.ts`, `list_pr_review_comments reads every page`) and the

- `bun run lint` (`tsc --noEmit` + `synth`) — clean; `dist/` is gitignored, nothing
  generated is committed.

Two behaviours changed deliberately, both in the direction #345 argued:

1. `pr-head-branch.ts` and `workspace-scope.ts` now **retry** a transient read. The

2. A pull request answered with **empty stdout** by `gh pr view` is now a failed read

needed for #345's other two acceptance criteria — #363 delivered the paging and the
merge-signals retry policy, and both are untouched here apart from sharing the new

{"status":"completed","exit_code":0,"stdout":"# The branch a run commits to

- A branch is created at the first commit, not at the start of a run. A run that
  only reports, confirms a merge, or closes an issue leaves no branch behind.
- The name is `atomaton/issue-N`. A merge deletes the branch, so the same issue's
  next piece of work takes that name again, cut fresh from the base branch.
- If a merged branch is still there — a deletion that failed, or a merge made
  some other way — the next name counts up instead: `atomaton/issue-N-2`, then
  `atomaton/issue-N-3`. Work never resumes on merged history.
- When an unmerged branch is left behind, the issue's next run resumes it
  instead of starting from the base branch.
- A sub-issue's branch is cut from its parent's and merges back into it, so
  sibling tasks see each other's work as it lands. The parent's branch is created
  from the base branch when the first child commits — until then it does not
  exist — and reaches the base branch as one pull request once every child is
  done. Deployment is not dispatched for a merge into a parent branch: that work
  is still in progress, and only the final pull request into the base branch
  carries it to release.
- The run is checked out on the base branch, so it learns where its work goes only
  at the first commit — by which time the parent's branch may have moved in the
  same files. The work is carried across as a three-way merge: the changes are
  stashed, the branch is cut from the parent, and `git stash pop` applies them to
  it. A file both sides changed is a conflict in the worktree, named, for the run
  to resolve before it commits; it is not a checkout that refuses because the tree
  is dirty, and no file the run did not touch keeps a base-branch version over the
  parent's. Both sides of a conflicted path are in git's index — `git show
  :2:<path>` is the version already on the branch, `git show :3:<path>` the one
  this run brings — and a text file holds git's markers in the worktree while a
  binary does not, so the run writes the side it wants into the file and names the
  path in `resolved_paths` on `commit_and_push`.
- A node's base is exactly one branch: its parent's, or the base branch for a root
  issue. When that branch moves ahead, the node brings it into its own branch with
  `merge_base_into_branch`. The direction is always a pull — nothing writes to a
  child's or a sibling's branch and nothing cascades, so two siblings catching up
  with the same parent never touch each other's work, and there is no shared state
  to keep consistent. A pull request run brings in the base its own pull request
  aims at, which is the same branch. It is also the route a stacked child takes to
  its parent's newer commits — the one it did not have before this.
- The base arrives as a merge commit, never as a rebase: the branch's own commits
  keep their hashes, and the merge records where it came from. A conflict stops it
  — nothing is committed, and both sides of each conflicted path stay in git's
  index — and the run resolves them and calls `commit_and_push` with
  `resolved_paths` naming each path to close the merge. Which side wins is
  the agent's decision; a version in `package.json` is the case that shows why no
  rule belongs there, since a machine choosing one could roll a release back
  quietly.
- A run's checkout is shallow — `actions/checkout` at its default
  `fetch-depth: 1` — so the branch's own ancestry stops at the one commit it
  checked out. `merge_base_into_branch` deepens the checkout to where the two
  histories meet before merging, so `refusing to merge unrelated histories` is
  never the answer to a merge base that only this clone had truncated.
- `sync_branch` is the other question and does not answer this one: it
  fast-forwards a branch to its own remote branch, and brings no base in.

Which branch the first of these is cut from is
[`base_branch`](../reference.md#base_branch), and the tree these branches follow is
[work is a tree of issues](work-is-a-tree-of-issues.md).

## Answers to "What to decide"

### 1. Should the three apply only when the base is the delivery branch?

**Recommendation: no as a blanket rule; exempt `merge.policy` and nothing else.**

- **`merge.policy` — exempt.** Its subject is a merge that leaves the tree, and it has no reading function: it does not say what to look at, only who merges. Under the default `manual` it is one human merge per child, which is the cost the issue names, and it is invisible here only because this repository is `auto`. This is the one exemption that is right on its own terms rather than on a trade-off.
- **`merge.governed_paths` — keep.** Its function is the read, and the read is real at the stacked level: the aggregate is a strictly worse first reading (4 files in #363, 12 in #368, against 64 in #371). Keeping it also keeps it one mechanism with gates, which `src/domain/delivery/merge-readiness.ts:424` states deliberately: "The project's own version of the gate above. Same shape, same outcome".
- **`merge.gates` — keep.** Measured cost 2 of 7, on exactly the change class this repository's own gate names, each a one-click merge after a review that found nothing. Against that: a person reading the merge-decision change as a 4-file diff instead of inside a 64-file aggregate.

**Alternative (rejected for now): exempt all three.** One predicate, one sentence in the docs, and the aggregate becomes the only place a person reads any of it. It is coherent, and if this project's gate ever costs more than 2 in 7 I would take it. Today it deletes the small-diff read on precisely the code that decides what an agent may merge, in exchange for a saving that is zero in this repository (`auto`) and unmeasured in any adopter.

### 2. If they apply to stacked merges, which of the three — and does the governed reasoning hold for gates?

Yes: the reasoning is the same for `governed_paths` and `gates`, because they are the same mechanism with different owners of the declaration (Atomaton's own default versus the project's `config.yaml`). What differs is only frequency, and that is measured above: gates 2 of 7, governed 0 of 7, policy 0 of 7.

The judgement point in scope — policy only, or all three in one change — is answered by that table: **policy only, in one change**; the other two need no behaviour change, only the doc sentence saying which merge they describe.

### 3. Where is the stacked merge's control, if not these checks?

It already exists and I measured all three legs:

1. **CI on every PR.** `pull-request-checks (verify)` concluded `success` on the heads of #348, #363, #368 and #371, with `default-branch-checks` skipped — the designed split between the PR's own secretless arm and the credentialed one.
2. **The reviewer agent on every PR.** Every one of the seven carries an `atomaton:agent=reviewer` comment; on the two gated ones it read the change and reported while leaving the merge.
3. **The parent's PR.** All three checks fire against the aggregate: #371 changed `src/adapters/github/merge-signals.ts`, matched the same gate, and a person merged it.

Plus `human-authored` (a person's PR is never merged by an agent) and the base branch's own rules, which are already read per branch (`src/adapters/github/merge-signals.ts:270`). **No new stacked-level mechanism is needed.**

### The spelling — and why not the one the issue proposes

`baseRefName === base_branch` fails in three ways that `isIssueBranch(baseRefName)` does not:

- **It fails open.** An unreadable base arrives as `""`; `"" !== "main"`, so the exemption would apply exactly when nobody knows what the base is. `isIssueBranch("")` is `false`, so the checks stay on.
- **It needs the base resolved.** `getBaseBranch()` returns `""` for the ordinary case, and turning that into a name is `baseBranch()` (`src/adapters/github/branch-reads.ts:163`) — a network read (`ls-remote --symref`) inside the merge path.
- **It exempts merges that are not work in progress.** A `release/1.x` or a person's branch is not the base branch, and `dispatchCd` **deploys** on a merge into those: it skips only issue branches (`src/adapters/actions/dispatch-targets.ts:289-296`). Those are the merges the three checks least want to exempt.

`isIssueBranch` (`src/adapters/github/branch-names.ts:46`) is already the predicate `dispatchCd` uses to answer exactly this question — is this merge a delivery? — and reusing it is what gives the rule one spelling, as the issue asks.

### Item 4, both sides: is a `.github/**` change on a stacked branch inert?

**For "inert", and it is measured:**
- The agent's own machinery is read from the default branch, not from the PR: `atomaton-runner.yml` checks out the default branch into `ATOMATON_MACHINERY_ROOT` and moves it out of the work tree (`.github/workflows/atomaton-runner.yml:177-186`), and `src/adapters/runner/machinery.ts:13-19` says why — "the runner sets the variable so a pull request cannot choose how the agent reviewing it behaves". So `config.yaml`, agent definitions and tool servers on a stacked branch change no run.
- A merge into an issue branch deploys nothing (`dispatch-targets.ts:289-296`), which is the repository already having decided, in the deploy path, that a stacked merge is not a delivery.

**Against "inert", and it is why I would not exempt it:**
- The read is the whole function of the governed gate; "no effect yet" is an argument about *what the change does*, and the three checks are about *who merges*. The governed read at stacked level is the only point where a person sees a `.github/**` change as the small diff it is.
- The PR's own CI arm is not inert: `atomaton-check` checks out "the pull request, whose commands these are" and plans from the PR's own `checks.from_pull_request` (`.github/workflows/atomaton-check.yml:26-38`), by design and secretless — but it means a `.github/**` change on a child is live for the validation of that child and of every sibling that later cuts from the parent.
