# Skill: project/conventions

# Repository conventions

This repository builds Atomaton, the delivery template. It is both the producer of
that template and an adopter of it, which creates rules that do not apply
anywhere else.

This file is not part of the template. Its source is `self/atomaton/skills/project/`,
and it is deliberately absent from `src/` so adopters never receive it.

## The four trees

| Tree | What it is | Who writes it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/**` | Source of the deliverable | You |
| `dist/.github/**` | The deliverable adopters receive | The build |
| `self/**` | This repository's own files, the ones that are not the template's | You |
| `.github/**` | This repository's running configuration | The self-deploy job, from a release plus `self/` |

Two different activities live in this table, and which one you are doing decides
which rules apply:

- **improving the deliverable** — `src/**`. It affects every adopter, and it
  reaches this repository only after a release and a self-deploy.
- **improving this repository's own operation** — `self/**`. It affects nobody
  else, and it applies as soon as it merges.

The rest of this file does not separate them cleanly. That is a known gap, tracked
in the documentation restructure; until then, read each rule and ask which of the two it is about.

`src/content/**` is mirrored verbatim into `dist/.github/atomaton/` and from there
into an adopter's repository. **It may only contain content that holds for any
project using Atomaton.** No reference to this repository's build pipeline, no
mention of `dist/`, `bun run synth`, or `build-dist.ts`, and no incident history
or PR numbers. If a rule is about developing *this* repository, it belongs in
this file instead.

## Generated output is not tracked

Change `src/**` only. `dist/**` is gitignored, so there is nothing generated to
commit and nothing to keep in sync.

Run `bun run synth` freely to inspect what adopters would receive. It writes only
into the ignored `dist/`, so it cannot dirty your commit.

Adopters receive the deliverable from a release, not from a merge, so nothing you
merge needs to carry it.

**Never touch `version` in `package.json`.** The version is the release declaration:
merging an edit to it publishes to adopters, and that decision belongs to a person,
made on the pull request the **Atomaton Release** workflow opens — never inside a
work pull request. A version left alone is a merge that publishes nothing, which is
the normal case. A work pull request that arrives with a version change in it is a
merge-blocking defect: flag it, and have the edit taken back out before merge.

`.github/**` is a different matter — see below. It is tracked, and every file in it
comes from either the release or `self/`.

## main is protected; everything lands by pull request

`.github/atomaton/rulesets/main.json` is the source of truth for what may reach main:
direct pushes are refused, and a pull request cannot merge until the `check` job
passes. It is applied by hand from an account with admin, and taken as correctly
configured thereafter — nothing verifies it, because a check could only report and
never enforce: with no ruleset, `check` would not be a required context either.

Changing the rule is a pull request against the JSON, followed by one `gh api`
call from an account with admin (see CONTRIBUTING.md). CI cannot make that call —
`administration` is not a permission a workflow can hold.

`check_merge_readiness` reports against whatever the ruleset currently
requires, so it follows the file rather than holding a second opinion.

Nothing bypasses it. No workflow writes to main — the release job attaches the deliverable
to a release instead — and your merge satisfies the rules like anyone else's. Do
not propose a bypass actor: it would mean naming a GitHub App ID or a deploy key,
values that exist only after manual setup, so the JSON would stop describing the
whole configuration.

The workflows that run agents are generated from `src/workflows/` and shipped.
`self/workflows/` holds the two that are not: `atomaton-self-deploy.yml` and
`probe-dumpable.yml`.

## Adding a static file to the deliverable

A new non-code file under `src/content/` must also be added to `build-dist.ts`'s
verbatim-copy list, or it never reaches `dist/` at all.
`tests/contract/deployment-contract.test.ts` enforces this.

## `atoma validate` is on the CLI

The `atoma` binary is on the agent's PATH — the runner installs it at
`/usr/local/bin/atoma` — and it has a `validate` subcommand that checks an agent
definition against a tools file without starting a run:

```bash
atoma validate --agent-def .github/atomaton/agent-definitions/engineer.md \
               --tools-file /tmp/tools.yaml
```

It resolves every name in the definition's `mcp_servers` against the tools file,
checks the template's placeholders, and reports what it finds. `atomaton-validate-pr`
runs it on every pull request that touches an agent definition, so a definition
that names a server `tools.yaml` does not define is a red check rather than a run
that aborts before a single tool starts.

There is no MCP tool for it, and that is deliberate: it is a check a person or a
workflow runs, not something an agent needs mid-run. Use it from the shell when
you are changing a definition and want the same answer CI will give.

## `.github/` is an adoption, not a mirror

Nothing regenerates `.github/` automatically. It is this repository's deliberate
adoption of the deliverable, so it lags `src/` until someone applies a release.

**That lag is the point.** A change to `src/` must not reconfigure the live agents
the moment it merges. Two breakages reached the running system exactly that way.

### Applying a release

Dispatch **Atomaton Self Deploy** (`self/workflows/atomaton-self-deploy.yml`) from the
Actions tab. It opens a pull request and merges nothing. `.github/**` is in
`merge.governed_paths`, so a person reviews it.

What it does:

```bash
rm -rf .github            # so a file the release DELETED is gone, not orphaned
unzip release.zip         # the deliverable
cp -r self/. .github/     # this repository's own, at the same paths
```

`.github/` is therefore exactly those two sources, with nothing kept alive by
remembering to. Before `self/` existed this was a `cp -r` followed by
`git checkout -- .github/atomaton/config.yaml`, and a file the template had removed
stayed in the tree with no diff to notice it by.

It needs `SELF_DEPLOY_TOKEN`, a PAT with the `workflow` scope, because
`GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot write `.github/workflows/**` — refused on identity, not by
path. No agent can reach that token: it is named in one file outside the
deliverable, and `atomaton-runner.yml` does not mention it.

### Changing something in `self/`

An overlay entry is a copy, not a build, so it needs no release. Change
`self/X` and `.github/X` **in the same pull request**, identically.

`tests/contract/self-overlay.test.ts` requires them byte-identical, in both
directions. Editing `.github/X` alone is worse than not editing it at all: the next
self-deploy overwrites it from `self/` and the change disappears without a diff.

A file added to `.github/` that is in no release and not in `self/` is not checked
for, because the next deploy removes it anyway and because `.github/**` is in
`merge.governed_paths` — no agent can merge a change there, so a person reads it first.

13	An agent will not merge a pull request that changes how agents run. It reviews
14	it and reports, and the merge is yours.

20	```
21	
22	A pattern is a literal path or a directory followed by `/**` — the same two forms
23	`merge.gates` accepts, and the only two.

28	merge:
29	  governed_paths:
30	    - ".github/**"

43	
44	`merge.governed_paths` covers Atomaton's own machinery. Your project has its own
45	things that should not land unread — a database migration, a change to a pricing

48	
49	`merge.gates` is that, and it behaves exactly like the gate above: the agent
50	reviews the pull request, posts the review, and says it is ready for a person.
51	The merge is yours.

54	merge:
55	  gates:
56	    - reason: "This adds a database migration. Please check it before merging."

61	`reason` is written to a person and relayed to them verbatim, in whatever
62	language you write it in. It is the whole output of the gate, so say what you

{"message": "Exempt a stacked merge from merge.policy, merge.governed_paths and merge.gates

A sub-issue's pull request merges into its parent issue's branch. That merge
delivers nothing: no deployment is dispatched for it, and what it becomes is the
parent's own pull request into the base branch, which carries the whole aggregate
and is where these three checks describe something real. Applying them at the
stacked level judged one change twice, the first time on a version that is not in
effect — and under the default `merge.policy: manual` it stopped every child for a
person, so a decomposition of five needed five human merges before the parent
could be judged at all.

The exemption is the pull request's base, read with `isIssueBranch(baseRefName)`:
the predicate `dispatchCd` already asks before deploying a merge, because it is
the same question. Comparing the base against the configured one instead would
fail three ways — an unreadable base arrives as "" and would exempt the merge
nobody knows the target of; resolving the configured base is a network read inside
the merge path; and a release branch or a person's branch is not the base branch
either, while a merge into one of those DOES deploy.

What covers a stacked pull request instead is what already covers every pull
request: its required check, its reviewer, and then the parent's pull request.
Not exempted: the commit-shaped blockers, and `human-authored`, so a person's
stacked pull request is still theirs to merge.

Both tools now say so in their answer (`stacked_merge`, and a note naming the
branch): "ready: true" with nothing else is indistinguishable from the three being
consulted and finding nothing, and that difference is why the merge needed no
person.

docs/pull-requests/reference.md states what a gate now promises — the small-diff
read of a gated change happens once, on the aggregate."}

Closes the decision on this issue: **all three merge-time checks stop applying to a pull request whose base is a work branch.** The principle, as decided: a check needed at merge time into main is done at merge time into main, and reading the same change twice is not a feature.

## What changed

- **`MergeSignals.stackedMerge`** (`src/domain/delivery/merge-readiness.ts`), set once in `gatherMergeSignals` with `isIssueBranch(baseRefName)` — the predicate `dispatchCd` already uses to decide a merge deploys nothing (`src/adapters/actions/dispatch-targets.ts:289-296`). One spelling of the work-branch convention; the domain stays pure and reads a fact, not a config.
- **One condition** wraps the five blockers those three checks produce: `merge-policy`, `governance-unknown`, `governance-change`, `merge-gate`, `gate-config-invalid`. `git diff -w` shows the whole domain change: the new field, one `if`, and the re-indent of the block it now contains.
- **Not exempted, deliberately:** every commit-shaped blocker (`draft`, `conflicting`, `behind`, checks failing/pending/missing, `mergeability-unknown`) and `human-authored` — a person's stacked pull request is still theirs to merge.
- **Both tools say so.** `check_merge_readiness` and `merge_pr` (refusal and every success shape) now carry `stacked_merge` and, when true, `stacked_merge_note` naming the base branch. `ready: true` with no explanation was indistinguishable from the three being consulted and finding nothing, which is the one thing a later reader cannot reconstruct.
- **Docs**: `docs/pull-requests/reference.md` (one statement shared by the three, one sentence in each section) and `docs/work/how-it-works/the-branch-a-run-commits-to.md`. The `merge.gates` section states what the gate now promises: the small-diff read of a gated change no longer happens at the stacked level, and `reason` is now written for a reader of the aggregate.

## Two judgement calls to check

1. **`gate-config-invalid` is exempt too.** It is the blocker that says a gate could not be evaluated, and it also carries "the changed files could not be read". Leaving it on would have blocked stacked merges for an unreadable file list while the gate that reads the same list was exempt — the same check reporting twice, once exempt and once not. A broken declaration still blocks every delivery merge.
2. **Why not `baseRefName === base_branch`**, as the issue first proposed: an unreadable base arrives as `""`, which is not the configured base, so the exemption would fire exactly when nobody knows the target (`isIssueBranch("")` is `false`, so the checks stay on); resolving the configured base is an `ls-remote` inside the merge path; and a release branch is not the base branch either, while a merge into one of those DOES deploy.

## Verification

- `bun run test` — **2129 pass, 0 fail** (169 files, 90s); `bun run typecheck` — clean; `bun run lint` (`tsc --noEmit` + `synth`) — clean, and `git status` after it shows only the eight edited files.
- `bun test tests/contract` — 496 pass. One caught a real slip: `no page under docs/ names self-deploy|SELF_DEPLOY_TOKEN` failed on my first wording ("a self-deploy's branch"), and the sentence was rewritten rather than the test.
- New tests, each measured against the code without the change:
  - `merge-readiness.test.ts` — "a stacked merge is not stopped by merge.policy, governed paths or a gate" and "a stacked merge is still refused for every reason that is not one of the three". With the wrapper forced open both fail; the second pins that the exemption is a condition and not a deletion.
  - `merge-signals.test.ts` — base `main` → `false`, `atomaton/issue-12` → `true`, `""` → `false`. The stacked one fails with `stackedMerge` forced to `false`; the `""` case pins the direction the rejected predicate gets wrong.
  - `mcp.test.ts` — "check_merge_readiness says a stacked merge skipped the delivery checks" runs under a config that sets no `merge.policy`, so the project default `manual` is in force and the answer is still `ready: true` with `blockers: []`; and `merge_pr`'s existing stacked fixture now asserts `stacked_merge: true` in its success payload. Both fail with the adapter's predicate forced to `false`.

<details><summary>What is not covered, and why</summary>

- No test exercises `governed_paths` or `gate-config-invalid` firing on a stacked merge for the obvious reason: they cannot any more. Their delivery-merge behaviour is covered by the existing tests, unchanged.
- The behaviour is decided in the domain, but nothing here measures a real stacked merge end to end — it would need a GitHub run with a gated child.
- The issue's own observed case (#363, #368) becomes agent-mergeable with this change, which is the intended outcome; I did not re-run either.

</details>

Not changed: `version` in `package.json`, and `.github/**` — this is a `src/` change and reaches the running configuration at the next self-deploy."}

- **Both tools say so.** `check_merge_readiness` and `merge_pr` (refusal and every success shape) now carry `stacked_merge` and, when true, `stacked_merge_note` naming the base branch. `ready: true` with no explanation was indistinguishable from the three being consulted and finding nothing, which is the one thing a later reader cannot reconstruct.
- **Docs**: `docs/pull-requests/reference.md` (one statement shared by the three, one sentence in each section) and `docs/work/how-it-works/the-branch-a-run-commits-to.md`. The `merge.gates` section states what the gate now promises: the small-diff read of a gated change no longer happens at the stacked level, and `reason` is now written for a reader of the aggregate.

## Two judgement calls to check

1. **`gate-config-invalid` is exempt too.** It is the blocker that says a gate could not be evaluated, and it also carries "the changed files could not be read". Leaving it on would have blocked stacked merges for an unreadable file list while the gate that reads the same list was exempt — the same check reporting twice, once exempt and once not. A broken declaration still blocks every delivery merge.
2. **Why not `baseRefName === base_branch`**, as the issue first proposed: an unreadable base arrives as `""`, which is not the configured base, so the exemption would fire exactly when nobody knows the target (`isIssueBranch("")` is `false`, so the checks stay on); resolving the configured base is an `ls-remote` inside the merge path; and a release branch is not the base branch either, while a merge into one of those DOES deploy.

## Verification

- `bun run test` — **2129 pass, 0 fail** (169 files, 90s); `bun run typecheck` — clean; `bun run lint` (`tsc --noEmit` + `synth`) — clean, and `git status` after it shows only the eight edited files.
- `bun test tests/contract` — 496 pass. One caught a real slip: `no page under docs/ names self-deploy|SELF_DEPLOY_TOKEN` failed on my first wording ("a self-deploy's branch"), and the sentence was rewritten rather than the test.
- New tests, each measured against the code without the change:
  - `merge-readiness.test.ts` — "a stacked merge is not stopped by merge.policy, governed paths or a gate" and "a stacked merge is still refused for every reason that is not one of the three". With the wrapper forced open both fail; the second pins that the exemption is a condition and not a deletion.
  - `merge-signals.test.ts` — base `main` → `false`, `atomaton/issue-12` → `true`, `""` → `false`. The stacked one fails with `stackedMerge` forced to `false`; the `""` case pins the direction the rejected predicate gets wrong.
  - `mcp.test.ts` — "check_merge_readiness says a stacked merge skipped the delivery checks" runs under a config that sets no `merge.policy`, so the project default `manual` is in force and the answer is still `ready: true` with `blockers: []`; and `merge_pr`'s existing stacked fixture now asserts `stacked_merge: true` in its success payload. Both fail with the adapter's predicate forced to `false`.

<details><summary>What is not covered, and why</summary>

- No test exercises `governed_paths` or `gate-config-invalid` firing on a stacked merge for the obvious reason: they cannot any more. Their delivery-merge behaviour is covered by the existing tests, unchanged.
- The behaviour is decided in the domain, but nothing here measures a real stacked merge end to end — it would need a GitHub run with a gated child.
- The issue's own observed case (#363, #368) becomes agent-mergeable with this change, which is the intended outcome; I did not re-run either.

</details>
